beats.visual: golden palace by the river Sarayu at dawn
beats.text: On the banks of the Sarayu stood Ayodhya, a city of peace and dharma. Its walls were high, its streets were wide, and no one in it ever went hungry.

beats.visual: busy streets of Ayodhya, merchants and elephants
beats.text: Merchants came from distant lands, elephants walked its roads, and the sound of the Vedas rose from every home.
Its king, Dasharatha of the Sun dynasty, had wealth, power and his people's love. He had three queens: Kausalya, Kaikeyi and Sumitra. But he had no son.

beats.visual: the king alone on a moonlit balcony, worried
beats.text: Who would carry the line of the Sun after him? The question kept the old king awake, night after night.
His guru, Sage Vasishtha, gave him hope. On his advice, the king invited the great sage Rishyasringa.
Together they performed the Putrakameshti Yagna, the sacred fire ritual for the blessing of sons.

beats.visual: a divine being rising from the flames with a golden bowl of kheer
beats.text: From the fire rose a shining being, holding a golden bowl. 'Share this kheer among your queens,' he said, 'and sons will be born to you.'

beats.visual: Dasharatha giving the kheer to his queens
beats.text: The king gave half to Kausalya, and shared the rest between Sumitra and Kaikeyi.
Soon, all three queens were with child. And so began the story that would shape the world.
In the month of Chaitra, on the ninth day, Queen Kaushalya gave birth to Rama, the embodiment of dharma. Today that day is celebrated as Ram Navami.

beats.visual: baby Rama glowing in a golden cradle
beats.text: Kaikeyi gave birth to Bharata. Sumitra gave birth to twins, Lakshmana and Shatrughna.
Ayodhya danced for days. Musicians played, and the king gave away cows and gold.

beats.visual: four boys playing in the palace garden
beats.text: The four grew up inseparable. Lakshmana's heart belonged to Rama, and Shatrughna's to Bharata. Lakshmana would not even eat unless Rama was beside him.
Under Sage Vasishtha they mastered the Vedas, archery, riding elephants and chariots, and the duties of a righteous king.
Yet Rama was loved for more than his skill. Even as a boy he was kind to everyone, and he always spoke first, with a smile.

beats.visual: Dasharatha watching his sons with pride
beats.text: The old king looked at his four sons and felt that every one of his prayers had been answered. He did not know how soon the world would come asking for them.
Demons were destroying the prayers of the sages. Every time a sacrifice began, they rained blood and flesh on the sacred fire.
The great sage Vishwamitra came to Ayodhya for help. Dasharatha promised him anything he wished.
'Send Rama with me,' said the sage. Rama was not yet sixteen. Dasharatha was heartbroken, and offered his whole army instead.
But Vasishtha reminded him: a king's word cannot be broken. So Rama and Lakshmana went willingly.

beats.visual: princes walking behind the sage along the river
beats.text: On the road, Vishwamitra taught them the mantras Bala and Atibala, so they would never feel hunger, thirst or tiredness, and then the secrets of divine weapons.

beats.visual: Tataka charging out of the forest
beats.text: Then came Tataka, a fearsome demoness with the strength of a thousand elephants, who had turned a whole land into a wilderness.
Rama hesitated to strike a woman, but the sage said a protector's duty comes first. Rama's arrow struck true. The forest was free again.

beats.visual: sages at a yagna, fire glowing
beats.text: At Siddhashrama, where Lord Vishnu himself had once meditated, Vishwamitra began a sacred yagna in silence.

beats.visual: Rama and Lakshmana standing guard at night
beats.text: Rama and Lakshmana guarded it for six days and nights without sleep, bows always strung.
On the last day, the altar burst into flames and the sky went dark. The demon Subahu and his general Maricha came roaring down, ready to pour blood onto the fire.
Rama did not panic. He fitted the Manava astra to his bow.
It struck Maricha in the chest and hurled him a hundred yojanas, far across the ocean. Rama had chosen not to kill him.
Then the Agni astra struck Subahu, and he fell. With the Vayu astra, Rama swept the rest of the demons away.
The yagna was complete. The sages were free, and they blessed the two young princes.

beats.visual: Maricha alone on a distant shore, trembling
beats.text: But far away, Maricha woke up on a lonely shore, shaking. He would never forget that arrow.

title: Ahalya
source: Valmiki, Bala Kanda 48-49 (the stone form comes from later retellings)

beats.text: On the road to Mithila, they found an empty ashram, silent for centuries. No bird sang there.
'This was the home of Sage Gautama,' said Vishwamitra. 'His wife Ahalya was the most beautiful woman the creator ever made.'

beats.visual: Indra in disguise at the hermitage
beats.text: 'One day, Indra came disguised as Gautama, and Ahalya was deceived. When the sage returned, he cursed them both.'
'She would live here unseen, living on air, doing penance, until Rama came.' Many later tellings say she was turned to stone.
As Rama entered, the curse broke. Ahalya appeared, radiant and free, shining like the moon behind clouds.

beats.visual: Rama and Lakshmana touching her feet
beats.text: Rama and Lakshmana bowed and touched her feet, as one honors a mother.

beats.visual: Ahalya bowing, flowers falling from the sky
beats.text: She bowed in gratitude. Flowers fell from the sky, and divine drums sounded.
Sage Gautama returned and took her back with honor. The empty ashram came alive again.
Rama had not fought anyone, yet he had won his gentlest victory. Her long penance had ended.
King Janaka of Mithila welcomed the princes with honor. He was a king and a sage at once, wise and gentle.

beats.visual: Janaka asking about the two princes
beats.text: He could not take his eyes off the two young men. 'Who are these princes, who walk like lions?' he asked.

beats.visual: a giant bow on an iron cart pulled by many men
beats.text: In his palace lay Shiva's mighty bow, so heavy that it took hundreds of men to pull it on its eight-wheeled cart. Not even gods and demons could lift it.

beats.visual: kings failing to lift the bow
beats.text: Many kings had come for it. Not one could even raise it off the ground.
Janaka had made a vow: whoever strings this bow will marry my daughter, Sita.
Vishwamitra turned to Rama and smiled. He knew exactly why he had brought Rama here.

beats.visual: Janaka telling the story of the bow
beats.text: Janaka told them its story. Long ago, Shiva had given this bow to Janaka's ancestor, and it had been worshipped ever since.

beats.visual: the bow's box being opened, golden light
beats.text: Now the great box was opened. Rama stepped closer, and the whole hall fell silent.

title: The Birth of Sita
source: Valmiki, Bala Kanda 66 (the casket and the bow as a toy are from later retellings)

beats.visual: Janaka ploughing a field at sunrise
beats.text: Years earlier, King Janaka was ploughing a field himself to prepare the ground for a sacred ritual.

beats.visual: the plough striking something in the earth
beats.text: Suddenly, the plough struck something hard in the soil.

beats.visual: a golden casket rising from the furrow
beats.text: From the earth emerged a glowing baby girl. Some tellings say she lay in a golden casket.
Janaka lifted her in his arms. He had no child of his own, and his heart filled with joy.

beats.visual: the baby in the palace, flowers around her
beats.text: He named her Sita, meaning 'furrow.' Born of the Earth, she was raised as his own daughter, and loved by all of Mithila.

beats.visual: young Sita lifting the heavy bow with ease
beats.text: Later tellings say that as a girl, she once moved Shiva's bow aside like a toy while cleaning the room.
Janaka saw it and knew she was no ordinary child. Only a man who could string that same bow would be worthy of her.

beats.visual: grown Sita in the palace garden
beats.text: Sita grew into a princess of grace and quiet strength, and kings from every land asked for her hand. Janaka refused them all, and waited.

title: The Swayamvar
source: Valmiki, Bala Kanda 67-73 (Ravana at the contest is from later retellings)

beats.text: Kings from across the land came to win Sita's hand. One by one, they failed. Some could not even move it.
In some later tellings, even mighty Ravana tried, and was crushed under the bow and left in shame.
Then Rama stepped forward. He bowed to his teacher, Vishwamitra, and walked to the bow.

beats.visual: Rama lifting the bow with one hand
beats.text: He lifted it as if it were light, and the whole court gasped.
As he drew the string to his ear, the bow broke in two, with a crack like thunder that shook Mithila. People fell to the ground in fear.
Janaka rose, tears in his eyes. 'My vow is fulfilled. Sita will marry Rama.'

beats.visual: Sita walking forward with a garland
beats.text: Sita walked forward slowly, her eyes lowered.
She placed the garland around Rama's neck, and the sky rained flowers.
Their eyes met for a moment. Ancient tellings say they were Vishnu and Lakshmi, finding each other again on earth.

beats.visual: Janaka sending a message to Ayodhya
beats.text: Janaka sent swift messengers to Dasharatha with the happy news.
Dasharatha arrived with his whole court, his army and his sages. The two kings embraced like brothers.

beats.visual: Janaka with his daughters and nieces
beats.text: Janaka made a joyful offer: his daughters and his nieces for all four princes.
Sita to Rama, Urmila to Lakshmana. Janaka's brother Kushadhwaja's daughters, Mandavi and Shrutakirti, to Bharata and Shatrughna.

beats.visual: the wedding hall decorated with banana leaves and lamps
beats.text: The wedding hall glowed with lamps, and the sages chanted as the auspicious hour arrived under the star Uttara Phalguni.
Four brothers married four sisters in one grand ceremony. They walked around the sacred fire together.

beats.visual: Sita and Rama at the fire
beats.text: As Janaka placed Sita's hand in Rama's, he said: 'She will follow you like your shadow.'
Flowers fell from the sky, and divine drums sounded.
His task complete, Vishwamitra blessed the couples and left for the Himalayas.
The whole city sang and danced for days. Janaka sent his daughters off with gold, silk, elephants and horses, and many tears.

beats.visual: the wedding procession on the road home
beats.text: On the way back to Ayodhya, a storm rose. The earth shook, and birds cried out.

beats.visual: Parashurama with his axe, eyes blazing
beats.text: A fearsome sage blocked the path. It was Parashurama, who had wiped out proud kings twenty-one times. His axe was on his shoulder.
Dasharatha begged him to spare his sons. Parashurama ignored him.
'You broke Shiva's bow,' he said to Rama. 'Now string Vishnu's bow, if you can.'
Rama took the bow, strung it, and fixed an arrow in one smooth motion.
'This arrow cannot go to waste,' said Rama. 'Shall I destroy your path, or the worlds you have won by your penance?'
Parashurama recognized the truth. He bowed, gave up his worlds to the arrow, and withdrew in peace.

beats.visual: the sky clearing, procession moving on
beats.text: The storm passed. Dasharatha held his son close, as if he had been born again.
The procession entered Ayodhya to music and joy, and the queens welcomed their four new daughters home.

title: The Coronation Plan
onscreen: Tomorrow, a king would be crowned…

beats.text: For twelve years, Ayodhya was happy under Dasharatha. Rama and Sita lived in joy, and the people adored their eldest prince.

beats.visual: the old king looking in a mirror at his white hair
beats.text: But the king was growing old. He had seen bad omens in his dreams, and his stars were turning against him.
He called his ministers and the kings of the land. 'I have served long enough,' he said. 'I wish to crown Rama as Yuvaraja, the heir to the throne.'
The whole court roared its approval. 'Rama is truthful, brave and kind,' they said. 'Crown him!'
Vasishtha fixed the ceremony for the very next morning, under the star Pushya. Bharata and Shatrughna were away at their uncle's kingdom.
News spread, and the city burst into celebration. Streets were sprinkled with water, flags flew from every roof, and lamps were lit through the night.

beats.visual: Rama and Sita fasting in prayer
beats.text: That night, Rama and Sita fasted and prayed to Lord Vishnu, sleeping on a bed of sacred grass.
Only Rama stayed quiet and humble. He never wanted the throne. He wanted only to serve.

beats.visual: Manthara on the palace roof watching the celebration
beats.text: From a palace terrace, a hunchbacked maid named Manthara watched the flags and flowers with a sour face.

beats.visual: Manthara asking why the city celebrates
beats.text: 'Why is the city rejoicing?' she asked. When she heard Rama would be crowned, she burned with anger and ran to her queen.
'Wake up, foolish queen! Rama becomes king tomorrow, and your son Bharata will be nothing. A servant to Rama for life.'

beats.visual: Kaikeyi giving Manthara a jewel in joy
beats.text: But Kaikeyi was delighted. She gave Manthara a jewel. 'Rama is like my own son,' she said.
Manthara threw it away. 'Remember the two boons the king once gave you, when you saved his life in the war against the demons?'
At first Kaikeyi loved Rama as her own son. But slowly, the poison of doubt took hold.

beats.visual: Kaikeyi removing her jewels, lying on the floor
beats.text: She tore off her jewels, put on soiled clothes, and lay on the bare floor of the anger chamber.

beats.visual: an empty dark chamber, a single lamp
beats.text: There she waited for the king. The happiest night of Ayodhya was about to become its darkest.
Dasharatha came looking for his favorite queen, and found her on the floor of the dark chamber, her hair loose and her jewels scattered.
'Who has hurt you?' he cried. 'Ask anything, and I swear by Rama, whom I love more than my life, I will give it.'
Kaikeyi rose. 'Two boons you promised me long ago. First: Bharata becomes king. Second: Rama goes to the forest for fourteen years, dressed as a hermit.'
The king fell to the ground as if struck by lightning. He begged, wept and pleaded. He even touched her feet.
'You are the king of the Ikshvaku line,' she said coldly. 'Will you break your word?' Kaikeyi did not move.

beats.visual: night passing, the king awake in grief
beats.text: The whole night passed. The king lay awake, calling Rama's name, praying that the dawn would never come.

beats.visual: dawn breaking over the decorated city
beats.text: Outside, the city woke up singing, ready for the coronation.
A king bound by his word. A father bound by love.

title: Rama Accepts Exile
onscreen: The kingdom lost. The dharma kept.

beats.visual: Rama arriving at the palace at dawn
beats.text: At dawn, Rama came to greet his father, expecting a blessing for his coronation. He found him broken, unable even to speak.
'What has happened, mother?' asked Rama. 'Have I displeased my father?'
Kaikeyi told him everything: the two boons, the throne for Bharata, the forest for him.
Rama did not argue or frown. 'If my father's word needs it, I go gladly,' he said. 'Why would I need the crown when I have his honor?'
He went to his mother Kaushalya. She fainted with grief, and begged to come with him.

beats.visual: Lakshmana in fury, hand on his sword
beats.text: Lakshmana raged and wanted to fight for the throne. Rama calmed him. 'This is destiny,' he said. 'No one is to blame.'

beats.visual: Rama removing his royal robes, putting on bark cloth
beats.text: Rama took off his silk and jewels and put on clothes of tree bark.

beats.visual: Rama walking away from the throne
beats.text: He gave up a kingdom as easily as one lets go of a flower.
Rama asked Sita to stay behind. 'The forest is hard and dangerous. There are snakes, wild beasts, thorns and demons.'
'Where you are is my home,' she said. 'Even a palace without you is a jungle. With you, the forest will be a garden.'
When Rama still refused, she wept and declared she would die rather than be left behind. At last, Rama agreed.
Lakshmana too refused to be left behind. 'I will walk ahead of you with my bow,' he said. 'I will serve you day and night.'
His mother Sumitra blessed him: 'Think of Rama as your father, Sita as your mother, and the forest as Ayodhya.'

beats.visual: three figures leaving the palace gate
beats.text: The three left Ayodhya in bark cloth, in the chariot of the minister Sumantra.

beats.visual: the whole city following in tears
beats.text: The whole city followed them in tears, running behind the chariot.

beats.visual: old Dasharatha falling in the dust
beats.text: Behind them, the old king fell in the dust, watching until the chariot was gone.

title: Guha and the Ganga
source: Valmiki, Ayodhya Kanda 46-52 (Kevat washing Rama's feet is from the Ramcharitmanas)

beats.visual: Rama leaving the sleeping citizens behind at night
beats.text: The people of Ayodhya would not turn back, so Rama left quietly at night while they slept.

beats.visual: a wide river at dawn, a boatman waiting
beats.text: At the Ganga, the boatman king Guha of Shringaverapura welcomed Rama as a dear friend.

beats.visual: Guha offering food and his kingdom
beats.text: He brought food and offered his whole kingdom. Rama refused gently. He had a vow to keep: no royal comforts for fourteen years.
Later tellings say the boatman washed Rama's feet before letting him in the boat, in case his touch turned the boat into a woman, as it had Ahalya.
Rama sent the minister Sumantra home with the empty chariot and a message of love for his father.
Guha rowed them across. Sita folded her hands and prayed to the Ganga for their safe return.

beats.visual: Rama cutting his hair into a sage's matted locks
beats.text: On the far bank, Rama and Lakshmana matted their hair with the sap of a banyan tree.

beats.visual: Rama dressed as a forest sage
beats.text: Here Rama gave up the last sign of royalty and became a forest sage.

title: Dasharatha's Death
onscreen: A father who died of love.

beats.text: With Rama gone, Ayodhya lost its light. No fires were lit, no songs were sung, and the markets were empty.

beats.visual: Sumantra returning with the empty chariot
beats.text: When Sumantra returned with the empty chariot, the king fainted.
Dasharatha cried Rama's name day and night. Then he remembered a curse from long ago.

beats.visual: young Dasharatha hunting by a river at night
beats.text: As a young prince, he had shot an arrow at a sound in the dark, thinking it was an elephant drinking.

beats.visual: the dying hermit boy with a water pot
beats.text: It was a young hermit filling a pot of water for his blind parents. Later tellings call him Shravan Kumar.

beats.visual: the old blind parents of the hermit
beats.text: The grieving parents cursed him: 'You too will die of grief, separated from your son.'

beats.visual: the king whispering in his last breath
beats.text: Now the curse had come true. On the sixth night, at midnight, he whispered, 'Rama, Rama,' and was gone.
At dawn, the queens found him still. The whole palace broke into cries.
Far away in his uncle's kingdom, Bharata had a terrible dream about his father.

beats.visual: Bharata riding home from his uncle's kingdom
beats.text: Bharata was away when all this happened. Messengers called him home in haste, without telling him why.
He felt something was wrong the moment he saw the silent city. No one greeted him. No one smiled.
Kaikeyi proudly told him: 'Your father is gone. Rama is in exile. The throne is yours.'
Bharata was shattered. 'You have destroyed my family for my sake? You are no mother of mine! I want nothing of this.'
He ran to Kaushalya, fell at her feet and swore he had known nothing of the plot.
He performed his father's last rites with Shatrughna, weeping beside the funeral fire.
When the ministers offered him the crown, he refused it. He set out to bring his brother home.

beats.visual: Bharata and the whole city marching into the forest
beats.text: Bharata led an army of citizens, queens and sages into the forest to find Rama.

beats.visual: Lakshmana seeing the army from a tree
beats.text: Seeing the army, Lakshmana thought Bharata had come to attack, and raised his bow. Rama stopped him. 'Bharata would never harm us.'
At Chitrakoot, Bharata found Rama's small hut. He fell at Rama's feet, weeping. 'Return and rule, brother.'

beats.visual: Rama learning of his father's death
beats.text: Then Rama learned that his father was dead. He wept, and offered water to his father's spirit at the river.
Rama embraced Bharata. 'Our father gave his word. I must keep it, and you must rule.'
Bharata would not give in. He sat outside the hut and vowed to fast until Rama agreed.

beats.visual: the sages watching the two brothers
beats.text: For hours, two brothers each tried to give the kingdom to the other. The sages watching had never seen such a contest.

beats.visual: the two brothers sitting face to face
beats.text: Neither would take the throne. Each only wanted the other to have it.
At last, Bharata asked for one thing. 'Give me your sandals.'

beats.visual: Rama placing his sandals in Bharata's hands
beats.text: Rama agreed. He stepped onto a pair of golden sandals and gave them to his brother.

beats.visual: Bharata carrying the sandals on his head
beats.text: Bharata carried them on his head all the way home, as if he were carrying Rama himself.
'If you do not return on the very day the fourteen years end,' he said, 'I will enter the fire.'

beats.visual: the sandals on the throne of Ayodhya
beats.text: He placed them on the throne and ruled in Rama's name, as a servant. Every decision was first laid before the sandals.

beats.visual: Bharata living in a simple hut at Nandigram
beats.text: He would not live in the palace. He lived in a simple hut at Nandigram, outside the city, wearing bark cloth and matted hair.
He lived like an ascetic for fourteen years, waiting for his brother.

beats.visual: Rama leaving Chitrakoot for the deeper forest
beats.text: And Rama, so that the people would stop coming, went deeper into the forest.
